title: Wide tables, OBT and lakehouse modelling
summary: How columnar engines changed the economics of joins and denormalisation: one big table, nested columns, activity schema and physical layout choices.

blocks.text: Star schemas were designed when row-oriented databases paid for every byte of every row scanned and joins were the main optimisation tool. Columnar storage (Parquet, ORC, Snowflake micro-partitions) reads only the columns a query touches and compresses repetitive values extremely well. That changes what denormalisation costs, and opens modelling options that were impractical before.

An OBT pre-joins a fact table with all its dimensions into a single wide table: one row per order line, with customer name, segment, product category, store region and date attributes as plain columns. Hundreds of columns are normal.

items: **Why it works on columnar engines**: a query selecting 5 of 300 columns reads only those 5. Repeated dimension values (a segment name repeated on 100 million rows) compress to almost nothing with dictionary and run-length encoding.
**Why consumers like it**: no joins means no wrong joins. BI tools, notebooks and LLM-generated SQL get one obvious table.
**Why it hurts**: dimension changes require rewriting history (a renamed category touches every row), the grain is frozen, and conformance across processes is lost if every team builds its own OBT.

blocks.text: Treat OBTs as a **serving artefact derived from a star**, not a replacement for it. Build conformed dimensions and facts in the model, then materialise OBTs in gold (chapter 15) for the consumers that need them. Rebuilding an OBT is cheap; rebuilding lost conformance is not.
11.2 Star schema vs OBT on columnar engines

Star schema
OBT / wide table

Column pruning makes width almost free

blocks.text: Benchmarks on modern warehouses often show OBTs somewhat faster for simple aggregations, and stars competitive once dimensions are small enough to broadcast. The difference is rarely large enough to decide the architecture alone; maintainability and semantic consistency usually matter more.

Columnar formats store nested types natively: Parquet and Iceberg support `struct`, `list` and `map`; Spark SQL exposes `STRUCT`, `ARRAY` and `MAP`; Snowflake has `VARIANT`, `OBJECT` and `ARRAY` plus structured types. Nesting lets you keep a parent and its children in one row, for example an order with an array of line items, without a join and without exploding the grain.

blocks.title: Nested order table (Spark SQL)
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE silver.orders_nested (
  order_id     STRING,
  customer_id  STRING,
  ordered_at   TIMESTAMP,
  shipping     STRUCT<city: STRING, country: STRING>,
  lines        ARRAY<STRUCT<sku: STRING, qty: INT, net_amount: DECIMAL(18,2)>>
) USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(ordered_at));

-- Order-level query: no explode needed
SELECT shipping.country, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM silver.orders_nested
GROUP BY shipping.country;

-- Line-level query: explode the array
SELECT l.sku, SUM(l.qty) AS units
FROM silver.orders_nested
LATERAL VIEW explode(lines) t AS l
GROUP BY l.sku;

blocks.title: Querying a VARIANT column (Snowflake)
blocks.text:
SELECT raw:order_id::STRING          AS order_id,
       raw:shipping.country::STRING  AS country,
       f.value:sku::STRING           AS sku,
       f.value:qty::INT              AS qty
FROM bronze.orders_json,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => raw:lines) f;

Semi-structured columns are excellent for landing and for genuinely variable payloads, but every consumer must know the paths and casts. Extract frequently queried paths into typed columns in silver. Engines can prune and compress typed columns far better than deeply nested or schemaless values; check your engine's documentation for how it sub-columnarises VARIANT or JSON.

The activity schema is an open specification that models an entity's behaviour as one long, narrow table of activities: `activity_id`, `ts`, `customer`, `activity` (a name such as `completed_order` or `opened_email`), generic features (three `feature_N` columns in version 1 of the spec, a `feature_json` column in version 2), `revenue_impact`, `link` and a precomputed `activity_occurrence` and `activity_repeated_at`. All business processes about a customer go into the same stream.

items: **Strength**: questions like *first touch before first purchase* or *orders within 7 days after a support ticket* become self-joins on one table with temporal predicates, instead of joins across many fact tables.
**Strength**: adding a new activity requires no new table, only a new transformation that appends rows.
**Weakness**: generic feature columns lose types and meaning; per-activity attributes need lookups. It complements, not replaces, dimensional models for finance-grade reporting.

blocks.text: In a lakehouse the physical layout is part of the model. Engines skip data using partition values and per-file min/max statistics (chapter 22). Good layout can turn a 10 TB scan into a 50 GB scan.

head: Choice
Good candidates
Avoid
rows: Low-to-medium cardinality, used in most filters: event day or month, region
High cardinality (user_id), producing thousands of tiny files
High-cardinality filter or join columns: customer_id, sku
Aim for partitions of at least hundreds of MB to a few GB
Hourly partitions on a table that gets 50 MB per day
days(ts), months(ts), bucket(N, id), truncate(L, s)
Deriving a separate date column users forget to filter on

blocks.text: Iceberg's hidden partitioning means users filter on `ordered_at` and the engine maps it to the `days(ordered_at)` partition automatically; chapter 23 covers partition evolution. Snowflake micro-partitions are created automatically, and an optional clustering key keeps large tables well ordered at extra compute cost. Databricks offers liquid clustering for Delta tables. Check the current documentation for each engine's specifics.

Partitioning by a column that is not in the query predicates gives no pruning but still multiplies file counts. Small files (a few MB each) are the most common lakehouse performance problem; see chapter 25 on compaction.

blocks.title: Product analytics on a lakehouse
blocks.text: A mobile app company landed 2 billion events per day. Analysts kept writing ten-way joins between events, users, devices and experiments. The team kept a conformed star in silver/gold, then published a daily `events_wide` OBT partitioned by `days(event_ts)` and sorted by `user_id`, with experiment assignments as an `ARRAY<STRUCT>` column.
items: Typical dashboard queries scanned one or two partitions and a handful of columns
Experiment analysis used `array_contains` instead of a join to a large assignment table
Renaming a device model required rebuilding only recent partitions, by policy

blocks.title: Choose a shape for subscription analytics
blocks.text: A streaming service needs: monthly revenue reporting for finance, churn-prediction features for data science, and a self-service table for product managers. Decide which consumers get a star, an OBT, nested columns or an activity stream, and propose partition and clustering keys for each physical table.
hints: Which consumer needs as-was history and reconciliation?
Which question is naturally about sequences of events per customer?

items: Columnar storage makes wide tables cheap to scan and store, which makes OBTs viable.
OBTs simplify consumption but freeze grain and history; derive them from a conformed star.
Nested structs and arrays keep parent-child data in one row; extract hot paths into typed columns.
Activity schema models behaviour as one temporal stream, good for sequence questions.
Partition on low-cardinality filter columns, cluster on high-cardinality ones, and avoid small files.

blocks.q: Why does a 300-column OBT not cost 300 columns of I/O for a query that uses 5 of them on a columnar engine?
options: The OBT is automatically split into a star
Only the referenced column chunks are read
The engine caches the whole table in memory
blocks.explain: Column pruning reads only the columns referenced. Columnar formats store each column separately within a row group or micro-partition, so unused columns are never read.

blocks.q: A product category is renamed (a type 1 change). Which model has the largest rewrite cost?
options: OBT with category name on every fact row
blocks.explain: In an OBT the category name is repeated on every fact row, so all affected rows must be rewritten. In a star you update one dimension row.

blocks.q: Which column is the worst partition key for a 5 TB events table?
blocks.explain: High-cardinality partition keys create millions of tiny files and huge metadata. user_id is a clustering or bucketing candidate, not a partition key.

blocks.q: What is the main strength of the activity schema?
options: It enforces strict typing of all attributes
It removes the need for partitioning
It replaces conformed dimensions for finance reporting
Temporal questions across many behaviours become queries on one table
blocks.explain: All activities of an entity share one stream, so cross-process sequence questions are self-joins with time predicates. It is weaker on typing and does not replace finance-grade dimensional models.
